replacement: “Let me ask your permission to drop this subject altogether,” Miüsov repeated. “Instead, gentlemen, I’ll tell you another interesting and fairly typical story about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Just five days ago, at a gathering here, mostly of ladies, he solemnly declared in the middle of an argument that nothing in the whole world makes people love their neighbors. He said there is no natural law that man should love mankind. If there has been any love on earth up to now, he said, it was not because of a natural law but only because men have believed in immortality. Ivan Fyodorovitch added in passing that the whole of natural law rests on that belief. Destroy mankind’s faith in immortality, he said, and not only love but every living force that keeps the world going would dry up at once. Moreover, nothing would be immoral then, and everything would be lawful, even cannibalism. And that’s not all. He finished by claiming that for every individual like ourselves, who believes neither in God nor in immortality, the natural moral law must at once turn into the exact opposite of the old religious law. Egoism, even to the point of crime, would become not merely lawful but recognized as the inevitable, the most rational, even the most honorable outcome of his situation. From this one paradox, gentlemen, you can judge the rest of the theories of our eccentric and paradoxical friend Ivan Fyodorovitch.”
“Speak without buffoonery, and don’t begin by insulting your own family,” answered the elder, in a weak, worn-out voice. He was plainly growing more and more tired, and his strength was failing.

“I thought ... I thought,” he said, in a soft, almost controlled voice, “that I was coming home with the angel of my heart, my betrothed, to cherish his old age. And all I find is a depraved libertine and a despicable clown!”

But this shameful scene was ended in the most unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly rose from his seat. Alyosha was nearly frantic with worry for the elder and for everyone else, but he managed to hold him up by the arm. Father Zossima walked toward Dmitri, and when he reached him he sank to his knees. Alyosha thought he had fallen from weakness, but he had not. The elder bowed down at Dmitri’s feet, clearly and deliberately, until his forehead touched the floor. Alyosha was so astonished that he did not help him up again. There was a faint smile on the elder’s lips.

Dmitri stood for a few moments, amazed. Bowing down to him—what did it mean? Suddenly he cried out, “Oh, God!” He covered his face with his hands and ran from the room. The guests all streamed out after him, so confused that they did not say good-by or bow to their host. Only the monks went up to him again for a blessing.
“Why not? I was specially invited yesterday.”

“Unfortunately I feel forced to go to this blasted dinner,” said Miüsov, with the same irritability, not caring that the monk was listening. “We ought at least to apologize for the disturbance, and explain that it wasn’t our doing. What do you think?”
“Yes, we should explain that it wasn’t our doing. Besides, father won’t be there,” Ivan said.
“Well, I should hope not! Blast this dinner!”
